A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same titled work by the same authors. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial methodological revision.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments in Tables 2–5, model-capacity analyses, and Fourier-domain robustness results in Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification results across multiple backbones, attention analyses, block ablations in Appendix C, and early training results in Appendix D.

M1.justification: v1 proposes T-STAtten and N-STAtten using cross-group attention followed by averaging across timesteps or tokens. v2 replaces these principal procedures with attention within contiguous temporal blocks, followed by concatenation. Section 4.3 also introduces integration with several transformer backbones while preserving their residual connections. This changes the attention computation, beyond renaming.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate static CIFAR10/100, sequential CIFAR10/100, ImageNet, CIFAR10-DVS and N-Caltech101. However, v1's frequency-filtered noisy-image evaluation scenario in Appendix D is removed. The additional backbone and block experiments otherwise use retained dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: The sequential comparison adds PLIF, Spikformer and SpikingReformer, the latter citing SpikingResformer. CIFAR and neuromorphic comparisons add SpikingReformer and QKFormer. ImageNet adds SDT-V2, SpikingReformer, QKFormer, ViT, DeiT and Swin, while the energy comparison adds quantized ViT. These methods participate in reported comparisons, rather than appearing only as citations.

E3.justification: v2 introduces entropy measurements, maximum-batch-size tests on a 24GB A5000, memory estimates at 32/8-bit precision, and ten-epoch ImageNet training comparisons. The attention-energy estimator changes from SK*SV+SQ to SK+SV+SQ. The standard SDT training budgets, splits and preprocessing remain largely unchanged between v1 Table 7 and v2 Table 8.

E4.justification: v1's Hamming-similarity, Grad-CAM and Fourier-noise analyses are removed. v2 adds entropy and neuronal-activity analyses, temporal-combination and block-size ablations in Tables 9–10, and early ImageNet training comparisons. The capacity study replaces CIFAR10-DVS with sequential CIFAR100 and adds spatial-only baseline results across model sizes.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, standard deviations, confidence intervals or significance tests, and neither displays uncertainty bars. v2's attention-entropy analysis measures feature concentration rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: Many result entries change: the sequential SDT baseline becomes 80.32/61.08 versus 76.67/51.75, while proposed SDT-based neuromorphic results become 81.1/83.15 versus 82.2/84.36. Reported ImageNet accuracies of 78.11/78.39 are retained, and SDT-V2 results of 79.85/80.67 are added. New ablation and memory results appear, and Appendix E revises layer energies. Changed methods and implementations limit direct performance comparisons.

T1.justification: v2 replaces the cross-group attention definitions with spatial, temporal and block-attention formulations, revises the analytical energy expression, and adds a binary-matrix argument for temporal neuron silencing in Appendix C.1. These are substantive mathematical changes. However, the displayed products in Eqs. 17 and 19 do not follow from their input matrices.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on T-STAtten and N-STAtten within SDT. v2 instead claims a general block-based module that improves multiple existing architectures while maintaining computational complexity. The contribution and applicability claims are substantially broadened, while the central claim that temporal context benefits spiking attention remains.

C2.justification: v2 motivates local temporal blocks through memory requirements, entropy and distant-timestep neuron silencing, replacing v1's similarity and Grad-CAM rationale. It removes the Fourier-filtering interpretation and adds block-size tradeoffs. New Section 5.5 explicitly acknowledges deployment difficulties on TrueNorth and Loihi despite block partitioning.

D1.justification: v2 specifies block sizes for static, neuromorphic and sequential evaluations, adds backbone-integration guidance, and identifies memory-test VRAM. The detailed SDT training, optimizer, hardware and augmentation recipes are largely retained. Additional backbones are referred to their original configurations; no code or data access change is reported.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around compatibility with SpikingResformer, QKFormer and SDT-V2, discussing their attention and residual designs. It adds entropy, quantized-transformer and heterogeneous-hardware literature, while removing references supporting v1's Grad-CAM, Fourier robustness and some temporal-motivation material.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodology, experimental narrative and conclusion are extensively rewritten around block processing and integration across architectures. Preliminary and architecture descriptions are reorganized, a limitations section is introduced, and the appendices are restructured around new ablations and training analyses.

P2.justification: The document adopts a two-column layout and substantially redesigns its displays. Attention diagrams are redrawn; similarity, Grad-CAM, overall-architecture and Fourier figures disappear; new heatmaps, entropy, memory and ablation displays appear. The energy plot becomes an expanded table, and benchmark tables highlight backbone–STAtten pairs.

improvement.justification: v2's broader backbone comparisons, targeted block ablations and explicit deployment limitations strengthen the paper. However, its new Appendix C.1 matrix examples are arithmetically incorrect, and revised Appendix E energies total about 12.72 mJ while Table 6 retains v1's 12.36 mJ. These new inconsistencies undermine central mechanism and efficiency arguments, making the net quality direction uncertain.
